python_lesson_1.title: Welcome to Python
python_lesson_1.description: Your first steps into the world of Python programming

python_lesson_1:slide:0.title: What is Python? 🐍
python_lesson_1:slide:0.content:
Python is one of the world's most popular programming languages. It's used by companies like Google, Netflix, and Instagram to build amazing software.

Python is known for being:
• Easy to read and write
• Powerful yet simple
• Perfect for beginners
• Used everywhere: web development, data science, AI, and more!

python_lesson_1:slide:1.title: Why Choose Python?
python_lesson_1:slide:1.content:
Python was designed to be simple and readable. Unlike other programming languages that use lots of symbols and brackets, Python uses plain English words.

Python powers:
🌐 Websites (Instagram, Pinterest)
🤖 AI and Machine Learning (Tesla, Spotify)
📊 Data Analysis (Netflix recommendations)
🎮 Games (Civilization IV)

python_lesson_1:slide:2.title: Your First Python Program
python_lesson_1:slide:2.content: Every programmer starts with "Hello, World!" - a simple program that displays text on the screen.

python_lesson_1:question:0.prompt: What makes Python special compared to other programming languages?
python_lesson_1:question:0.explanation: Python's main strength is its readability and simplicity, making it perfect for beginners while still being powerful enough for experts.

options.python_lesson_1:question:0:option:0: It's easy to read and write

python_lesson_1:question:1.prompt: Which command displays text in Python?
python_lesson_1:question:1.explanation: The print() function is used to display text output in Python.

python_lesson_1:question:2.prompt: What punctuation must surround text in print()?
python_lesson_1:question:2.explanation: Text (strings) in Python must be wrapped in quotes - either single '' or double "".

python_lesson_1:question:3.explanation: Python is used by many major companies including Google, Netflix, Instagram, Spotify, and more!

python_lesson_1:question:4.prompt: Python is called an interpreted language. What does that mean?
python_lesson_1:question:4.explanation: Python code is run by an interpreter, which executes it directly without a separate compile step in day-to-day workflows.

options.python_lesson_1:question:4:option:0: Code is executed line by line by an interpreter
options.python_lesson_1:question:4:option:1: Code is only executed after manual translation to C
options.python_lesson_1:question:4:option:2: Code can only run inside a browser
options.python_lesson_1:question:4:option:3: Code cannot be reused in projects

python_lesson_1:question:5.prompt: What defines a code block in Python instead of curly braces {}?
python_lesson_1:question:5.explanation: Python uses indentation to define blocks, making structure explicit and readable.

python_lesson_1:question:6.prompt: Which command installs a third-party Python package?
python_lesson_1:question:6.explanation: pip is Python’s package manager, and pip install installs packages from package indexes.

python_lesson_1:question:7.prompt: What is the output type of this expression: 3.14?
python_lesson_1:question:7.explanation: Values with a decimal point are floating-point numbers (float).

python_lesson_1:question:8.prompt: Why is Python often recommended for beginners?
python_lesson_1:question:8.explanation: Python’s clean syntax and rich libraries make learning and building projects easier.

options.python_lesson_1:question:8:option:3: It has no errors at runtime

python_lesson_1:question:9.prompt: What is the common file extension for Python files?
python_lesson_1:question:9.explanation: Python source files are typically saved with the .py extension.

challenge.title: Say Hello!
challenge.description: Write a program that displays "Hello, Python!" to the screen.
challenge.hint: Use the print() function to display text. Remember to put your text in quotes!

python_lesson_2.title: Variables - Storing Information
python_lesson_2.description: Learn how to store and use data in your programs

python_lesson_2:slide:0.title: What are Variables? 📦
python_lesson_2:slide:0.content:
Think of variables like labeled boxes that store information. You can put different types of data in these boxes and use them later.

For example:
• A box labeled "name" might contain "Alice"
• A box labeled "age" might contain 25
• A box labeled "is_student" might contain True

python_lesson_2:slide:1.title: Creating Variables
python_lesson_2:slide:1.content: In Python, creating a variable is super simple! You just write the name, an equals sign, and the value.

python_lesson_2:slide:2.title: Types of Data
python_lesson_2:slide:2.content:
Python automatically understands different types of data:

• Text (String): "Hello", "Python", "123 Main St"
• Numbers (Integer): 5, 42, -10, 0
• Decimal Numbers (Float): 3.14, 2.5, -1.2
• True/False (Boolean): True, False

python_lesson_2:slide:3.title: Using Variables
python_lesson_2:slide:3.content: Once you create a variable, you can use it anywhere in your program by writing its name.

python_lesson_2:question:0.prompt: How do you create a variable called "score" with the value 100?
python_lesson_2:question:0.explanation: In Python, you create variables using the assignment operator (=). Just write: score = 100

python_lesson_2:question:1.prompt: What type of data is "Hello World"?
python_lesson_2:question:1.explanation: Text in quotes is called a String. "Hello World" is a string because it contains text characters.

python_lesson_2:question:2.prompt: Which of these is a valid variable name?
python_lesson_2:question:2.explanation: Variable names can contain letters, numbers, and underscores, but cannot start with a number or contain hyphens.

python_lesson_2:question:3.prompt: What is the value of x after: x = 5; x = 10?
python_lesson_2:question:3.explanation: Variables can be reassigned. The second assignment (x = 10) replaces the first value.

python_lesson_2:question:4.prompt: What type is the value True?
python_lesson_2:question:4.explanation: True and False are Boolean values - they represent yes/no or on/off states.

python_lesson_2:question:5.prompt: Which variable name follows Python naming conventions?
python_lesson_2:question:5.explanation: Use letters, numbers, and underscores; don’t start with a number or use keywords.

python_lesson_2:question:6.prompt: What is the difference between = and == in Python?

python_lesson_2:question:7.prompt: What is y after this code? x = 10; y = x; x = 20
python_lesson_2:question:7.explanation: y stores the value x had at assignment time, so y remains 10.

python_lesson_2:question:8.prompt: What type is the value True in Python?
python_lesson_2:question:8.explanation: True and False are boolean values (bool).

python_lesson_2:question:9.prompt: How do you convert the string "42" to an integer?
python_lesson_2:question:9.explanation: int("42") parses the numeric string and returns the integer 42.

challenge.title: Personal Info Card
challenge.description:
Create two variables:
• name = "Alex"
• age = 25

Then print each on separate lines:
Name: Alex
Age: 25
challenge.hint: Replace the comments with values: name = "Alex" (with quotes for text) and age = 25 (no quotes for numbers).

python_lesson_3.title: Math in Python
python_lesson_3.description: Learn to do calculations and work with numbers

python_lesson_3:slide:0.title: Python is a Great Calculator! 🔢
python_lesson_3:slide:0.content: Python can perform all basic math operations and much more. You can use it like a powerful calculator!

python_lesson_3:slide:1.title: Math with Variables
python_lesson_3:slide:1.content: You can use variables in math operations, making your calculations dynamic and reusable.

python_lesson_3:slide:2.title: Special Math Operations
python_lesson_3:slide:2.content: Python has some special math operators that are really useful:

python_lesson_3:slide:3.title: Updating Variables
python_lesson_3:slide:3.content: You can change a variable's value by assigning it a new value. You can even use the variable's current value to calculate the new one!

python_lesson_3:question:0.explanation: ** is the power operator. 10 ** 3 means 10 to the power of 3, which is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.

python_lesson_3:question:1.prompt: If x = 5, what will x += 3 make x equal to?
python_lesson_3:question:1.explanation: x += 3 is shorthand for x = x + 3. So if x starts at 5, it becomes 5 + 3 = 8.

python_lesson_3:question:2.explanation: The % operator (modulo) returns the remainder after division. For example, 17 % 5 = 2.

python_lesson_3:question:3.explanation: // is floor division - it divides and rounds down to the nearest whole number. 15 / 4 = 3.75, but 15 // 4 = 3.

python_lesson_3:question:4.prompt: Which operator has the highest priority (executes first)?
python_lesson_3:question:4.explanation: Python follows math order of operations: ** (power) is calculated first, then * and /, then + and -.

python_lesson_3:question:5.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence, so 3 * 4 is done before addition.

python_lesson_3:question:6.prompt: What is the difference between / and // in Python?
python_lesson_3:question:6.explanation: / keeps decimals, while // floors the result to an integer-like value.

options.python_lesson_3:question:6:option:0: / returns float division, // returns floor division
options.python_lesson_3:question:6:option:1: / returns integer division, // returns float division
options.python_lesson_3:question:6:option:3: / is for strings, // is for numbers

python_lesson_3:question:7.prompt: Which expression checks if n is even?
python_lesson_3:question:7.explanation: An even number leaves remainder 0 when divided by 2.

python_lesson_3:question:8.explanation: round(value, 2) keeps two digits after the decimal point.

python_lesson_3:question:9.explanation: abs returns the absolute (non-negative) magnitude of a number.

challenge.title: Calculate Circle Area
challenge.description: Given a radius, calculate the area of a circle using the formula: area = 3.14 * radius * radius
challenge.hint: Use the formula: area = 3.14 * radius * radius. Remember that radius * radius is the same as radius ** 2.

python_lesson_4.title: Working with Text
python_lesson_4.description: Master text manipulation and string operations

python_lesson_4:slide:0.title: Strings are Powerful! 📝
python_lesson_4:slide:0.content: In programming, text is called a "string" because it's like a string of characters tied together. Python has many tools to work with text.

python_lesson_4:slide:1.title: Combining Text (Concatenation)
python_lesson_4:slide:1.content: You can join strings together using the + operator, just like adding numbers!

python_lesson_4:slide:2.title: Useful String Methods
python_lesson_4:slide:2.content: Strings come with built-in "methods" - special functions that can transform them:

python_lesson_4:slide:3.title: F-strings: The Modern Way
python_lesson_4:slide:3.content: F-strings are the most elegant way to combine text and variables in Python:

python_lesson_4:question:0.prompt: How do you combine "Hello" and "World" with a space between?
python_lesson_4:question:0.explanation: To combine strings with a space, use: "Hello" + " " + "World" which gives "Hello World".

python_lesson_4:question:1.explanation: The .upper() method converts all letters to uppercase, so "python" becomes "PYTHON".

python_lesson_4:question:2.explanation: F-strings start with f and use {variable_name} syntax: f"Hello {name}"

python_lesson_4:question:3.explanation: len() returns the number of characters in a string. "Python" has 6 characters.

python_lesson_4:question:4.prompt: How do you get the first character of text = "Hello"?
python_lesson_4:question:4.explanation: Use square brackets with index. In Python, indexing starts at 0, so text[0] is the first character.

python_lesson_4:question:5.explanation: Slicing starts at index 1 and stops before index 4: y, t, h.

python_lesson_4:question:6.explanation: strip removes leading and trailing whitespace from a string.

python_lesson_4:question:7.explanation: split creates a list by cutting the string at each separator.

python_lesson_4:question:8.explanation: join places the separator between each list element.

python_lesson_4:question:9.explanation: Strings cannot be modified in place; create a new string instead.

challenge.title: Build a Username
challenge.description: Create a username by combining first name, last name initial, and birth year.
challenge.hint: Use string concatenation (+) or an f-string. To get the first letter of last_name, use last_name[0]. Convert birth_year to string with str().

python_lesson_5.title: Making Decisions
python_lesson_5.description: Learn how programs make choices using if statements

python_lesson_5:slide:0.title: Programs That Think! 🤔
python_lesson_5:slide:0.content:
Real programs need to make decisions based on different situations. The "if" statement lets your program choose what to do.

Think of it like:
"IF it's raining, bring an umbrella"
"IF the score is high, show congratulations"

python_lesson_5:slide:1.title: Basic If Statement
python_lesson_5:slide:1.content: The if statement checks if something is true, then runs code only if it is:

python_lesson_5:slide:2.title: If-Else: Two Choices
python_lesson_5:slide:2.content: Use else to handle the case when the condition is false:

python_lesson_5:slide:3.title: Multiple Conditions
python_lesson_5:slide:3.content: Use elif (else if) to check multiple conditions:

python_lesson_5:slide:4.title: Comparison Operators
python_lesson_5:slide:4.content: These operators help you compare values:

python_lesson_5:question:0.prompt: What happens if the condition in an if statement is false?
python_lesson_5:question:0.explanation: When an if condition is false, Python skips all the code inside that if block.

options.python_lesson_5:question:0:option:1: The code inside the if block is skipped

python_lesson_5:question:1.explanation: == checks if two values are equal and returns True or False. Don't confuse it with = which assigns values.

options.python_lesson_5:question:1:option:1: Checks if two values are equal

python_lesson_5:question:2.prompt: Which keyword is used for "otherwise" in Python?
python_lesson_5:question:2.explanation: The "else" keyword handles the case when the if condition is false.

python_lesson_5:question:3.prompt: What happens if no condition is True and there is no else?
python_lesson_5:question:3.explanation: If no condition matches and there is no else block, Python simply skips the entire if statement.

python_lesson_5:question:4.explanation: != checks if two values are NOT equal. Example: 5 != 3 returns True.

python_lesson_5:question:5.prompt: What is the result of: (5 > 2) and (3 < 1)?
python_lesson_5:question:5.explanation: The first condition is True, the second is False; True and False is False.

python_lesson_5:question:6.explanation: The in operator checks membership, and "py" is a substring of "python".

python_lesson_5:question:7.prompt: Which expression is Python’s ternary conditional form?
python_lesson_5:question:7.explanation: Python uses value_if_true if condition else value_if_false.

python_lesson_5:question:8.prompt: Why does the order of if / elif conditions matter?
python_lesson_5:question:8.explanation: Python evaluates top to bottom and executes the first true branch.

options.python_lesson_5:question:8:option:0: Python checks all branches and picks random one
options.python_lesson_5:question:8:option:1: First matching branch runs, later branches are skipped

python_lesson_5:question:9.explanation: 4 > 1 is True, and not True becomes False.

challenge.title: Age Category Checker
challenge.description: Write a program that categorizes people by age: Child (0-12), Teen (13-19), Adult (20-64), Senior (65+)
challenge.hint: Use if-elif-else with age ranges. Check from youngest to oldest or use appropriate comparison operators.

python_lesson_6.title: Working with Lists
python_lesson_6.description: Learn to store multiple items in ordered collections

python_lesson_6:slide:0.title: What are Lists? 📝
python_lesson_6:slide:0.content:
Lists let you store multiple items in a single variable. They are ordered, changeable, and allow duplicate values.

Real-world examples:
• Shopping list
• Playlist of songs
• List of high scores
• Todo items

python_lesson_6:slide:1.title: Creating Lists
python_lesson_6:slide:1.content: Lists are created using square brackets [], with items separated by commas.

python_lesson_6:slide:2.title: Accessing List Items
python_lesson_6:slide:2.content: Access items by their index number. Python uses zero-based indexing (first item is 0).

python_lesson_6:slide:3.title: List Methods
python_lesson_6:slide:3.content: Python provides many built-in methods to modify lists.

python_lesson_6:question:0.prompt: Which index accesses the first element?
python_lesson_6:question:0.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing: index 0 is the first element.

python_lesson_6:question:1.prompt: Which method adds an item to the end?
python_lesson_6:question:1.explanation: append() adds a single item to the end of a list.

python_lesson_6:question:2.prompt: What does fruits[-1] return if fruits = ["a", "b", "c"]?
python_lesson_6:question:2.explanation: Negative indexing starts from the end. -1 is the last item, -2 is second to last, etc.

python_lesson_6:question:3.prompt: How do you change the second item in a list?
python_lesson_6:question:3.explanation: The second item has index 1 (since indexing starts at 0). Use list[1] = value to change it.

python_lesson_6:question:4.explanation: Slice [1:3] starts at index 1 and ends before index 3.

python_lesson_6:question:5.prompt: What is the difference between append and extend?
python_lesson_6:question:5.explanation: append adds a single object; extend iterates and adds each element.

options.python_lesson_6:question:5:option:0: append adds one item, extend adds each item from an iterable
options.python_lesson_6:question:5:option:1: append removes item, extend adds item
options.python_lesson_6:question:5:option:2: append sorts list, extend reverses list

python_lesson_6:question:6.prompt: How do you insert "x" at index 1 in list a?
python_lesson_6:question:6.explanation: insert(index, value) adds an item at a specific position.

python_lesson_6:question:7.prompt: What does nums.pop() do by default?
python_lesson_6:question:7.explanation: pop() without index removes and returns the last element.

options.python_lesson_6:question:7:option:1: Removes last element and returns it

python_lesson_6:question:8.prompt: What is [x * x for x in [1, 2, 3]]?
python_lesson_6:question:8.explanation: List comprehension applies x * x to each element in the list.

python_lesson_6:question:9.prompt: How do you copy a list to avoid shared references?
python_lesson_6:question:9.explanation: original.copy() (or original[:]) creates a shallow copy with separate list object.

challenge.title: Shopping List
challenge.description:
Create a list with these 3 items: "milk", "bread", "eggs"
Then add "butter" to the list.
Finally, print the total count (should be 4).
challenge.hint: Use shopping.append("butter") to add an item, then print(len(shopping)) to print the count.

python_lesson_7.title: Loops and Iteration
python_lesson_7.description: Repeat actions efficiently with for and while loops

python_lesson_7:slide:0.title: The for Loop 🔄
python_lesson_7:slide:0.content: Loops let you repeat code multiple times. The for loop iterates over sequences.

python_lesson_7:slide:1.title: The range() Function
python_lesson_7:slide:1.content: range() generates sequences of numbers for loops.

python_lesson_7:slide:2.title: The while Loop
python_lesson_7:slide:2.content: while loops continue as long as a condition is True.

python_lesson_7:question:0.explanation: range(3) generates 0, 1, 2 (up to but not including 3).

python_lesson_7:question:1.explanation: break immediately exits the current loop.

python_lesson_7:question:2.explanation: range(2, 8, 2) starts at 2, ends before 8, step 2 → gives 2, 4, 6.

python_lesson_7:question:3.prompt: Which keyword skips to the next iteration?
python_lesson_7:question:3.explanation: continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.

python_lesson_7:question:4.prompt: What is wrong with: while True: print("Hi")?
python_lesson_7:question:4.explanation: Since the condition is always True, this loop never stops - it is an infinite loop!

python_lesson_7:question:5.prompt: What does enumerate(["a", "b"]) produce in a loop?
python_lesson_7:question:5.explanation: enumerate provides both index and element during iteration.

python_lesson_7:question:6.prompt: In a while loop, what is necessary to prevent accidental infinite loops?
python_lesson_7:question:6.explanation: The loop condition must eventually become false, often by updating a counter/state variable.

options.python_lesson_7:question:6:option:0: Update variables involved in the condition
options.python_lesson_7:question:6:option:1: Always use break in first line

python_lesson_7:question:7.prompt: What is the difference between break and continue?
python_lesson_7:question:7.explanation: break ends the loop immediately; continue jumps to the next cycle.

options.python_lesson_7:question:7:option:0: break exits loop, continue skips current iteration
options.python_lesson_7:question:7:option:1: break skips iteration, continue exits loop

python_lesson_7:question:8.explanation: range starts at 1, increments by 3, and stops before 10.

python_lesson_7:question:9.prompt: How many total iterations occur in two nested loops: for i in range(2), for j in range(3)?
python_lesson_7:question:9.explanation: Outer loop runs 2 times and inner loop runs 3 times each: 2 * 3 = 6.

python_lesson_8:slide:0.title: What are Dictionaries? 🗂️
python_lesson_8:slide:0.content:
Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs. Each key is unique and maps to a value.

Like a real dictionary:
Word (key) → Definition (value)

In programming:
"name" → "Alice"
"age" → 25

python_lesson_8:slide:1.title: Creating Dictionaries
python_lesson_8:slide:1.content: Use curly braces {} with key:value pairs.

python_lesson_8:slide:2.title: Dictionary Methods
python_lesson_8:slide:2.content: Useful methods for working with dictionaries.

python_lesson_8:question:0.prompt: How do you access a dictionary value?

python_lesson_8:question:1.explanation: The keys() method returns all dictionary keys.

python_lesson_8:question:2.prompt: What happens if you access a key that does not exist?
python_lesson_8:question:2.explanation: Accessing a non-existent key raises a KeyError. Use .get("key") to safely return None instead.

python_lesson_8:question:3.explanation: Dictionary keys must be immutable (unchangeable). Lists can change, so they cannot be keys.

python_lesson_8:question:4.prompt: What does user.get("role", "guest") return if role is missing?
python_lesson_8:question:4.explanation: get with a default value returns that default when key does not exist.

python_lesson_8:question:5.prompt: How do you update or add key "age" with value 30 in dict d?
python_lesson_8:question:5.explanation: Assigning with brackets creates the key or updates existing value.

python_lesson_8:question:6.prompt: Which loop gives both key and value?
python_lesson_8:question:6.explanation: items() returns key-value pairs, which can be unpacked in the loop.

python_lesson_8:question:7.prompt: What happens with duplicate keys in a dictionary literal?
python_lesson_8:question:7.explanation: Dictionary keys are unique; later duplicate assignments replace earlier values.

python_lesson_8:question:8.prompt: Which key type is valid for dictionaries?
python_lesson_8:question:8.explanation: Keys must be hashable (immutable types like tuples are allowed; lists/dicts/sets are not).

python_lesson_8:question:9.explanation: pop removes the specified key and returns its value.

options.python_lesson_8:question:9:option:0: Returns value for "name" and removes the key

python_lesson_9:slide:0.title: What are Functions? ⚙️
python_lesson_9:slide:0.content:
Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform specific tasks.

Benefits:
• Avoid code repetition
• Organize complex programs
• Make code easier to test
• Enable code sharing

python_lesson_9:slide:1.title: Defining Functions
python_lesson_9:slide:1.content: Use the def keyword to create functions.

python_lesson_9:slide:3.title: Return Values
python_lesson_9:slide:3.content: Functions can return values using return.

python_lesson_9:question:0.explanation: The def keyword defines functions in Python.

python_lesson_9:question:1.prompt: What does a function return by default?
python_lesson_9:question:1.explanation: Functions without return statements return None.

python_lesson_9:question:2.prompt: What is wrong with: def greet(name): return f"Hi {name}" print("Done")?
python_lesson_9:question:2.explanation: return exits the function immediately. Code after return is unreachable.

python_lesson_9:question:3.explanation: Parameters are variables that receive values when the function is called.

python_lesson_9:question:4.prompt: What is the output? def add(a=2, b=3): return a+b; print(add())
python_lesson_9:question:4.explanation: Default parameters are used when no arguments are provided.

python_lesson_9:question:5.prompt: What is the advantage of keyword arguments?
python_lesson_9:question:5.explanation: Keyword arguments improve readability and let you pass values by name.

options.python_lesson_9:question:5:option:0: They make calls clearer and allow reordering
options.python_lesson_9:question:5:option:1: They run faster than positional arguments
options.python_lesson_9:question:5:option:2: They remove need for return statements
options.python_lesson_9:question:5:option:3: They are only for recursive functions

python_lesson_9:question:6.prompt: What happens if you access a local variable outside its function?
python_lesson_9:question:6.explanation: Local variables are scoped to the function body and are unavailable outside it.

python_lesson_9:question:7.prompt: What does *args collect in a function definition?
python_lesson_9:question:7.explanation: *args packs additional positional arguments into a tuple.

python_lesson_9:question:8.prompt: How can a function return multiple values in Python?
python_lesson_9:question:8.explanation: Python packs comma-separated return values into a tuple.

options.python_lesson_9:question:8:option:1: Return values separated by commas (tuple packing)

python_lesson_9:question:9.prompt: Where is a function docstring typically written?
python_lesson_9:question:9.explanation: A docstring is usually the first string literal inside a function.

options.python_lesson_9:question:9:option:1: As first statement inside the function body
options.python_lesson_9:question:9:option:2: At the end of file only

python_lesson_10.title: Handling Errors
python_lesson_10.description: Deal with errors gracefully in your code

python_lesson_10:slide:0.title: What are Exceptions? ⚠️
python_lesson_10:slide:0.content:
Exceptions are errors that occur during program execution.

Common exceptions:
• ZeroDivisionError (divide by 0)
• ValueError (wrong value type)
• TypeError (wrong data type)
• FileNotFoundError (missing file)

python_lesson_10:slide:1.title: Try and Except
python_lesson_10:slide:1.content: Handle errors with try/except blocks to prevent crashes.

python_lesson_10:slide:3.title: Finally Block
python_lesson_10:slide:3.content: Code in finally always runs, whether an error occurred or not.

python_lesson_10:question:0.explanation: The except block catches and handles exceptions.

python_lesson_10:question:1.prompt: When does the finally block execute?
python_lesson_10:question:1.explanation: finally always executes, regardless of errors.

python_lesson_10:question:2.prompt: What exception occurs when dividing by zero?
python_lesson_10:question:2.explanation: ZeroDivisionError is raised when you try to divide a number by zero.

python_lesson_10:question:3.prompt: How do you catch any exception?
python_lesson_10:question:3.explanation: except Exception: catches most exceptions. You can also use except: alone to catch all.

python_lesson_10:question:4.prompt: When handling multiple exceptions, why should specific except blocks come before except Exception?
python_lesson_10:question:4.explanation: A broad except Exception would catch specific errors first and hide targeted handlers.

options.python_lesson_10:question:4:option:3: General exception runs only in debug mode

python_lesson_10:question:5.prompt: When does the else block in try/except/else run?
python_lesson_10:question:5.explanation: else executes when the try block succeeds without exceptions.

options.python_lesson_10:question:5:option:1: Only if no exception occurs in try block

python_lesson_10:question:6.prompt: What is a good use case for finally?
python_lesson_10:question:6.explanation: finally is ideal for cleanup actions that must always run.

python_lesson_10:question:7.prompt: How do you intentionally raise a ValueError?
python_lesson_10:question:7.explanation: Use raise with an exception type (and optional message).

python_lesson_10:question:8.prompt: What is better practice for production code: bare except or specific exception types?
python_lesson_10:question:8.explanation: Specific catches are safer and avoid masking unrelated bugs.

python_lesson_10:question:9.prompt: If int(user_input) can fail, where should conversion be placed?
python_lesson_10:question:9.explanation: Put risky operations in try and handle expected errors with matching except blocks.

options.python_lesson_10:question:9:option:0: Inside try block with ValueError handler
